newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GERMANY MOURNS END OF BECKER GOLDEN ERA.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GERMANY MOURNS END OF BECKER GOLDEN ERA.

text.p: Germany mourned the beginning of the end of a golden era of tennis after national favourite Boris Becker announced his retirement from top-level competition following defeat in a Wimbledon quarter-final.
"A German hero who has inspired us for 12 years is leaving the stage," wrote Cologne's Express daily on Friday. "In the press conference after his last Wimbledon match he made us all sad."

Becker, who dived into Wimbledon history by winning the men's singles title as a 17-year-old in 1985, confirmed he had played his final match at the All England Club on Thursday and said he would not compete in any more grand slam tournaments after this year.
"For German tennis this means that the player who has attracted most of the attention worldwide has gone," said Jens-Peter Hecht, spokesman for the German Tennis Federation.
"This is a great disappointment for the fans but I am sure they will understand his decision. He has played at the top for so long, had so much success and done so much good for tennis.
"We have had an exceptional situation over the last 10 years with Becker, Steffi Graf and Michael Stich too, which we definitely won't see again," Hecht said.

Stich, always overshadowed by Germany's favourite redhead, made it to the Wimbledon semifinals with a smooth victory over Britain's Tim Henman on Thursday but he too has said this Wimbledon will be his last and he will retire at the end of the year.

Graf, who is recovering from a knee operation and is not at Wimbledon to defend her title, has also said she is considering ending her career. After Wimbledon she will drop to number five or six in the world rankings, her worst position for 11 years.

Becker's defeat by world number one Pete Sampras may prove to be his last grand slam appearance. He has yet to decide whether he will compete in this year's U.S. Open and after that will restrict himself to smaller tournaments and the Davis Cup.
"Frustrated, without strength, smashed on his beloved grass by opponent Pete Sampras -- Boris Becker as we have never seen him before," lamented Express.

Becker's shock triumph at the 1985 Wimbledon, followed by the rise of Graf and Stich, fuelled a tennis boom in Germany with sponsors throwing money at the sport and the men's game bringing two of the most important tournaments -- the ATP world championship and the Grand Slam Cup -- to the country.
Andreas Schmidt, editor of the TV Today television magazine, says Germany is now seeing the end of the explosion in tennis popularity.
"In 1984, the year before the first Becker triumph in Wimbledon, German television offered a total of 13 hours of live tennis," he wrote in a column for the Kicker sports magazine.
"By 1992 we had 2,739 hours and since then it has sunk year by year to 1,658 hours now."
German television channel RTL decided soap operas would earn them more advertising revenue than Wimbledon would this year and will broadcast the final live only if Stich is playing.
Players and officials fear the waning interest of German fans and sponsors could hurt the sport as a whole.
Becker was so concerned that he decided to find his own successor and approached one of his sponsors, German luxury car-maker Mercedes-Benz, to help launch a junior men's team.
One of Becker's prodigies, 19-year-old Nicholas Kiefer, made it to the quarter-finals on his Wimbledon debut but went out to Australian Todd Woodbridge on Thursday.
"I am sure that German tennis will continue to have success with players like Kiefer and Thomas Haas," said Hecht. "But there is a real hole in women's tennis without Graf."
